opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest shift is that the bar for "knowing how" is dropping really fast, while the bar for "knowing what" and "knowing why" is going up.

For a long time, doing something great required years of accumulated craft: you had to learn the tools, the syntax, the techniques, the tedious parts of a field before you could even get to the interesting questions. A lot of that is now compressible. If I want to try an idea in a domain I'm not trained in, I can get a working prototype much faster than before, because the model fills in a lot of the procedural knowledge for me.

But that doesn't mean you need to know less. It means the knowledge that matters moves up a level. You need taste: the ability to look at ten outputs and know which one is actually good, which one is subtly wrong, and which one is pointing at something new. You need judgment about which problems are worth working on, because when execution gets cheap, choosing the wrong problem becomes the dominant failure mode. And you need enough real understanding of the fundamentals to catch the model when it's confidently wrong. If you can't verify, you can't really build on top of it.

The other thing I'd say is that breadth becomes more valuable. Many great ideas come from connecting two fields that don't usually talk to each other. Before, the cost of becoming even moderately competent in a second or third field was high. Now you can get to a working level in an adjacent area much faster, so the people who are curious and willing to roam across disciplines have a real advantage.

So my short answer is that AI lowers the cost of execution and raises the premium on taste, judgment, and asking the right question. The scarce thing is no longer "can you do it," but "do you know what's worth doing, and can you tell when it's actually been done well."

r001.rationale: The response says AI makes execution cheaper and raises the value of taste and judgment, but does not claim that knowing what a great result looks like is sufficient; it also emphasizes problem selection and understanding fundamentals to verify outputs.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that AI changes it less than people assume, and in a direction that surprises them.

Before, the bottleneck for doing something great was often execution knowledge. You wanted to build a product, you had to know how to code. You wanted to publish research, you had to know statistics, you had to know how to write. The gap between having a good idea and being able to act on it was enormous, and most of what we called "expertise" was really the accumulated ability to close that gap.

AI compresses that gap. It doesn't eliminate it, but it shrinks it dramatically. So the natural assumption is: great, now you need to know less. And that's partly true at the level of skills.

But what you need to know more of is taste. Judgment. You need to know what a good outcome looks like, because now you can generate ten plausible outcomes in an afternoon and you have to pick. When execution was expensive, you only got one shot, so the question of "is this the right thing" was almost a luxury. You were busy just getting it to work. Now the right-thing question is the whole job.

And I'd push further. The thing you most need to know now is the thing you can't ask the model, because the model gives everyone the same answer. Any question that has a knowable answer, the answer is now cheap for everybody. So the edge moves to what's not knowable yet. What do you believe about the world that most people don't? What have you seen firsthand that isn't in the training data? What problem do you care about enough to stay with it after the easy version is done?

So I'd say: you need to know less about how, and much more about why and what. And honestly, the second kind of knowing was always what separated great from good. AI just removed the excuse of being stuck on the first kind.

r001.rationale: The response says knowing what a good outcome looks like matters more as AI makes execution cheaper, but it does not claim that this knowledge alone is sufficient to achieve the result. It also says AI does not eliminate the execution gap.

astra-6.text:
I think AI shifts what you need to know from how to execute every step toward knowing what’s worth doing and what good looks like. You can start building something without mastering every tool first, because AI can help you fill in those gaps as you go.

But that makes judgment more important. If you can generate ten different solutions quickly, you still need to understand the problem well enough to choose between them. Is this actually useful? Is it correct? What are we missing?

So I’d say you need enough depth to question the answers, and enough curiosity to explore beyond what you already know. AI makes it easier to produce something. Doing something great still requires you to care about the details and understand the people you’re doing it for.

r001.rationale: The response says knowing what good looks like matters and AI can help fill execution gaps, but it also says greatness requires judgment, depth, curiosity, and understanding people. It does not claim that knowing the desired result is sufficient when AI handles execution.

sol-6.1.text:
I think AI changes the balance between knowing how to do something and knowing what’s worth doing. You can get help writing code, exploring an idea, or learning a technique much faster now. But you still need enough understanding to ask good questions and judge whether the result is any good.

So if you want to do something great, I think taste and judgment become more important. What problem do you choose? What does success actually look like? Where might the answer be wrong? AI can help you move faster, but you have to decide whether you’re moving in a useful direction.

And you still have to engage with the world. Build something, put it in front of people, see what happens. It’s easy to mistake a convincing conversation about an idea for progress on the idea. The real learning comes when you try it.

r001.rationale: The response says judgment about success matters, but also says you need understanding and must build and test ideas. It does not claim that knowing what a great result looks like is sufficient when AI handles execution.
